entries.clue: (& 20dn.) Republican blind to truth, i.e. contender lie-spreading (8)

indicatorNotes.spreading: the letters of the fodder are spread about and laid out afresh

annotation.surface: A swipe at a Republican candidate who refuses to accept the truth and spreads lies.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs on into 20 across. Fodder and indicator are fused in 'lie-spreading', which reads as one satirical compound.
annotation.definitionFit: An election denier is a Republican who refuses to accept a lost vote, blind to the truth of the count.

entries.clue: Eye never starts to get litigious, follow? (5)

indicatorNotes.starts: the starts of words are their first letters

blocks.note: first letters of Eye and Never
to sue is to get litigious

annotation.surface: Private Eye (the magazine) being threatened with a lawsuit and wondering if one will follow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eye' looks like the magazine setting this puzzle, which is under near-constant legal threat; here it only donates its E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what comes after, especially as a result, is said to ensue.

entries.clue: Once popped the question in the nude? (7)

blocks.note: to pose a question is to put it

annotation.surface: Someone who once proposed marriage without any clothes on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Popped the question' is the stock phrase for a marriage proposal, but here it just means asked a question: posed.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone in the nude is exposed, with nothing covered.

entries.clue: What right-wing press would call Boris's sacking – yet Archer wobbles (9)

annotation.definition: What right-wing press would call Boris's sacking

indicatorNotes.wobbles: the letters wobble out of their order

annotation.surface: Tory newspapers crying betrayal over Boris Johnson's fall, while Jeffrey Archer, the disgraced Tory novelist, wavers.
annotation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer is a Conservative peer and novelist jailed for perjury; he is only fodder here.
annotation.definitionFit: The pro-Johnson papers framed his removal by his own party as treachery.

entries.clue: Surpass someone else's shag tally for a cost? (6)

blocks.note: a jokey verb on the model of outrun and outdo: beat a rival at getting laid

annotation.surface: A boast about beating a rival's tally of sexual conquests, whatever it costs.
annotation.walkthrough: OUT-LAY: 'lay' is slang for a sexual partner or act, and 'shag' is British slang for sex. The question mark flags the invented verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the money you lay out on something is its cost.

entries.clue: Mad Putin all but resolved to invade Switzerland's borders (6)

indicatorNotes.all but: all but the last letter is kept
indicatorNotes.resolved: the letters are resolved into a new order
indicatorNotes.borders: the borders of a word are its first and last letters

blocks.note: PUTIN without its last letter, PUTI, rearranged

annotation.surface: Putin as a madman poised to cross the Swiss frontier.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mad Putin' reads as one noun phrase, but 'Mad' is the definition standing alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Mad in the sense of foolish or idiotic: stupid.

entries.clue: Date – score second time (5)

blocks.note: a try is a score in rugby

annotation.surface: Hoping to score on a second date.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Score second time' reads as a hope for the date's ending; the rugby sense of score is the one used.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the romantic sense: a secret meeting arranged between lovers.

entries.clue: Old European kingdom puts pressure on aggressive power (7)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, on means on top of, so P sits above and comes first

annotation.surface: A historical kingdom leaning on a belligerent neighbour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Puts pressure on' reads as leaning on; here it is placement, P sitting on top of RUSSIA.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this north German state was a monarchy from 1701 until 1918.

entries.clue: Wrecker Tory's about to be clad in fawn? (9)

indicatorNotes.to be clad in: the rearranged letters are dressed in the outer word

blocks.note: first part of DEER; a fawn is a young deer
the rest of DEER, wrapped round

annotation.surface: A Tory wrecker about to be dressed in beige, or dressed in deerskin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fawn' reads as the colour; the question mark admits the stretch from a young deer to DEER.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one who wrecks, with a nod to the warship sense.

entries.clue: Presume maligned Diana was one (7)

indicatorNotes.maligned: the letters are badly treated, knocked out of order

annotation.surface: A presumption that Princess Diana was badly treated by the press.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface points at Princess Diana, but the Diana meant is Diana Ross, lead singer of the Supremes.
annotation.definitionFit: A general-knowledge definition: Diana Ross sang lead in the Motown trio, so she was a member of it.

entries.clue: Smart panties brandished (7)

indicatorNotes.brandished: waved about, so the letters are thrown out of order

annotation.surface: Someone waving a pair of smart knickers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smart panties' reads as fancy underwear; 'Smart' is the definition in its clever sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the Latin for wise; smart here is the clever sense, not the well-dressed one.

entries.clue: Increase what you have and get stuffed (2,5)

annotation.surface: Advice to grow your holdings, followed by a rude brush-off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Get stuffed' and 'up yours' are both British rude dismissals.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are coarse ways to tell someone to go away.

entries.clue: Laid back presiding officer's seat (4,5)

blocks.note: the chair presides over a meeting

annotation.surface: A relaxed Speaker lounging in the official chair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Presiding officer's seat' reads as one phrase; the 's is 'is', so the chair is the person, and 'seat' stands alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: an upholstered armchair is one kind of seat.

entries.clue: Stunner, in fact a servant (5)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer is in the letters that follow

annotation.surface: A beautiful woman who is in fact a servant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stunner' reads as a beautiful person; a Taser stuns with an electric shock.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the police weapon fires darts carrying an electric shock that stuns its target.

entries.clue: Dick's short rule Mark overturned (6)

indicatorNotes.short: the word is cut to its abbreviation

blocks.note: reg = short for regulation, a rule

annotation.surface: A Dick whose brief rule was overturned by a Mark.
annotation.walkthrough: Todger is British slang for penis; 'Dick' looks like a name, next to 'Mark'.
annotation.definitionFit: Dick and todger are both slang for penis.

entries.clue: Everyone in Tunbridge Wells outskirts is onto Conservative lie (4,5)

indicatorNotes.in: ALL goes in the outer letters
indicatorNotes.outskirts: the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters
indicatorNotes.is onto: TORY is attached onto the end

annotation.surface: Everyone in the suburbs of Tunbridge Wells falling for a Tory falsehood.
annotation.walkthrough: Tunbridge Wells is a Kent spa town, a byword for comfortable Tory-voting England. Its outskirts are the ends of the whole name, T and S.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: an exaggerated, hard-to-believe account, close enough to an untruth.

entries.clue: Is my arse suitable for an agent of the state? (8)

indicatorNotes.suitable: the letters are made suitable, fitted into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether their backside is good enough for a state agent.
annotation.walkthrough: The rude surface question hides the fodder in plain sight: 'Is my arse' holds all eight letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a representative sent abroad on a government's behalf.

entries.clue: Leader Lance – nut! (9)

annotation.surface: An insult hurled at a leader called Lance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lance' looks like a man's name and 'nut' like an insult; they are a weapon and a head.
annotation.definitionFit: The spearhead is the leading part of an attack, or the person leading it.

entries.clue: Don't be so exploitative – it's futile (7)

annotation.surface: A plea to stop exploiting people, dismissed as pointless.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half splits the answer into two words, USE LESS.
annotation.definitionFit: Useless and futile both mean achieving nothing.

entries.clue: Philatelist possibly changes first for one seeking to manipulate member (8)

indicatorNotes.changes first: the first letter is changed for another

blocks.note: stamp collecting is one hobby, so a philatelist is a hobbyist

annotation.surface: A stamp collector switching careers to become a political fixer.
annotation.walkthrough: The replacement L is not clued; the crossing letters and definition supply it. 'Member' is a Member of Parliament.
annotation.definitionFit: A lobbyist tries to sway MPs, members of parliament.

entries.clue: Roll over Beethoven initially composed with Erich (7)

indicatorNotes.composed: the letters are composed into a new arrangement

blocks.note: o = over, as on a cricket scorecard

annotation.surface: The rock song 'Roll Over Beethoven', written by a composer called Erich.
annotation.walkthrough: The song title swallows the definition: 'Roll' is the bread, and 'over' is just O.
annotation.definitionFit: A brioche is a sweet French bread roll.

entries.clue: see 1dn.
E.J. Thribb's contributions are so contrary (7)

blocks.note: Thribb is a poet, so his contributions take the form of poems

annotation.surface: A remark that a poet's pieces are perverse.
annotation.walkthrough: E.J. Thribb (17½) is Private Eye's fictional teenage poet, who writes obituary poems beginning 'So. Farewell then'. His work is IN VERSE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the mathematical and logical sense of turned the opposite way.

entries.clue: Rather opportune, Scotland's international body (6)

indicatorNotes.Rather: loosely, only rather (partly) the letters are used

annotation.surface: A timely reference to Scotland's place on the world stage.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the comma, which a solver reading for sense skips over.
annotation.definitionFit: UNESCO is the United Nations' educational, scientific and cultural organisation.

entries.clue: Clubs, etc for despised white-collar executives? (5)

blocks.note: clubs, hearts, diamonds and spades: the four groups in a pack of cards
a sneering name for corporate managers, from their business clothes

annotation.surface: A golf club full of hated corporate bosses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' suggests golf or nightclubs where executives gather; it is the card suit.
annotation.definitionFit: Both the card groups and the besuited managers are suits.

entries.clue: Foreign head involved in crap move (5)

indicatorNotes.head: the head of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.involved in: F is wrapped up inside the other word

blocks.note: the rest of SHIT, wrapped round F

annotation.surface: A foreign leader caught up in a rubbish political manoeuvre.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Foreign head' reads as a foreign head of state; it is the first letter of 'Foreign'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verb or noun: to shift furniture is to move it, and a shift is a move.

entries.clue: Country finished if Republican gets in – this will get you over the rough (9)

annotation.definition: this will get you over the rough

indicatorNotes.gets in: R gets in between the other letters

annotation.surface: A warning that the nation is done for if a Republican takes power.
annotation.walkthrough: A Land Rover is a British four-wheel-drive vehicle built for rough ground; 'rough' also nods at golf.
annotation.definitionFit: An off-road vehicle carries you over rough terrain.

entries.clue: Old characters' energy overwhelmed by diarrhoea (5)

indicatorNotes.overwhelmed by: E is engulfed by the surrounding word

blocks.note: first part of RUNS; 'the runs' is slang for diarrhoea
the rest of RUNS, wrapped round E

annotation.surface: Some elderly people laid low by a stomach bug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old characters' reads as old folk; the characters are letters of an ancient alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: Runes are the letters of old Germanic alphabets.

entries.clue: Bloomers inspire minors with dread, you might say (7)

indicatorNotes.you might say: what you might say out loud, not how it is written

blocks.note: awe = inspire with dread; kids = minors

annotation.surface: Old-fashioned knickers frightening children.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' reads as baggy underwear; the flower sense is the definition. The sound match relies on a non-rhotic British accent.
annotation.definitionFit: Orchids are flowering plants, things that bloom.

entries.clue: Inaugurate US president Don, steeped in evil? (5,2)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition carries its object: to swear in a president is to inaugurate one

indicatorNotes.steeped in: WEAR is steeped inside the other word

blocks.note: first letter of SIN; sin = evil
to don is to put on, wear
the rest of SIN, wrapped round WEAR

annotation.surface: Donald Trump, sworn in as president, soaked in wickedness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Don' is Donald Trump in the surface and the verb 'don' in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with its object: a president takes office by taking the oath before a judge.

entries.clue: Secretary of State, yet dithering about check (6)

indicatorNotes.dithering: the letters dither, shuffling out of place
indicatorNotes.about: they go round the other word

blocks.note: first letter of YTE, the anagram of YET, split round the check

annotation.surface: A cabinet minister hesitating over a decision.
annotation.walkthrough: Yvette Cooper is a senior Labour cabinet minister; a first name as the answer is unusual, fair only because she is so well known.
annotation.definitionFit: Yvette Cooper has served as Home Secretary and Foreign Secretary, both Secretaries of State.

entries.clue: You'll be glad to hear this goes down swimmingly (4,4)

annotation.definition: You'll be glad to hear this

indicatorNotes.swimmingly: the letters swim about into a new order

annotation.surface: Something welcome that is received very well.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Goes down swimmingly' is British for being very well received, so the whole clue reads as one idiom; the fodder is hiding in it.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: welcome tidings are what a listener is glad to hear.
